items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public health law, in relation to establishing the
nightlife opioid antagonist program
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8633

SPONSOR: COMRIE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to establishing the
nightlife opioid antagonist program

 
PURPOSE:

To establish the voluntary night-life opioid antagonist program and
prevent needless opioid overdose deaths in night clubs.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 creates a new section 3309-b to the public health law, requir-
ing the Commissioner of the Department of Health to establish a night-
life opioid antagonist program, and establishes definitions to include
"nightlife establishment" as inclusive of businesses such as bars,
clubs, and restaurants, and defines "opioid antagonist" to include
narcan, naloxone, and other FDA-recognized opioid overdose treatments
found by medical professionals to reduce or prevent death.

Section 2 creates the program whereby a nightlife establishment can
receive an opioid antagonist in line with existing law, free of charge,
and directs the health department to publish participating establish-
ments online for public view.

Section 3 establishes eligibility criteria to include compliance with
requirements of this section, and that applications shall be submitted
either by mail or online.

Section 4 sets approval via satisfying the requests stated above. It
also requires that an application that is initially declined by the
commissioner result in notification to the applicant as to their defi-
ciencies in writing to encourage reapplication without prejudice.

Section 5 makes clear that there will be no fee for participating estab-
lishments.

Section 6 states participating establishments would receive a maximum of
10 doses and report to the department when doses were discharged, wheth-
er because of an actual emergency as stated by the purpose of the
program, an accidental discharge, or if a dose is no longer effective.
Additionally, the antagonist is non-transferrable and must be used at
the participant establishment that applied to the program.  The commis-
sioner will set forth rules and regulation as needed.

Section 7 grants the department commissioner the power to withdraw
participants from the program in the event their participation poses a
danger to public health, safety, or welfare, provided that after such
suspension an opportunity for hearing shall be provided on an expedited
basis. An establishment whose participation has been suspended may reap-
ply with proof that disqualifying issues have been remedied.

Section 8 requires the department offer the staff of participant estab-
lishments necessary resources and training on overdose prevention and
the administration of opioid antagonists provided by this program. It is

stated that only staff who have received such training are authorized to
administer the on-site antagonist.

Section 9 makes clear that the state has no liability associated with
the administration of the program at these voluntarily participating
establishments.

Section 10 provides that every March 1" beginning 2023 from the effec-
tive date of this bill's passage that the department will provide infor-
mation on the administration of the program to the office of the gover-
nor and leaders of both houses of the state legislature. Such a report
shall include the total number of doses provided to each establishment,
the number of times a dose was discharged, and the number of times a
dose was improperly discharged.

Section 2 establishes an effective date 120 days after passage.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

This bill will authorize training and put life-saving treatment into the
hands of nightlife establishment employees, similar to AEDs.  Nightlife
establishments are one of many everyday contexts in which statistics
tell us opioids are consumed at a higher frequency. This program seeks
to bring overdose prevention to as many responsibly-minded bars and
nightclubs as possible - especially as they recognize that beyond the
intentional consumption of opioids themselves, people who consume other
drugs, including cocaine, crack, heroin, methamphetamine, ketamine, and
pills from various sources are potentially exposed to fentanyl. Anyone
who uses drugs that may contain fentanyl, even occasionally, is at risk
of a fatal overdose.

An opioid antagonist is a life-saving treatment that rapidly reverses an
opioid overdose. When administered to someone in need, it attaches to
opioid receptors in their body and reverses and blocks the effects of
other opioids. Narcan, naloxone, and similar FDA-approved opioid antag-
onists have been proven to restore normal breathing to a person if their
lung and heart function has dramatically slowed or stopped due to an
opioid overdose; it can often make the difference between life and
death.

In addition to providing opioid antagonist training for nightlife work-
ers and making these treatments more readily available to people across
the state, this program will supplement existing educational and aware-
ness programs to reduce senseless overdose deaths and curb the consump-
tion of drugs by New York residents.

In 2018, the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
(DOHMH) collaborated with the Brooklyn Allied Bars & Restaurants (BABAR)
to reach bar and nightclub owners as well as staff to begin an overd -e
prevention pilot program. This intervention was part of the overall
comprehensive plan by the City of New York to address the recent opioid
crisis in both its own jurisdiction and across the state, given its
location as a central gathering place for recreation and entertainment.
After showing initial success, the program was expanded in 2019.

This bill finds parity with an existing bill of the New York City Coun-
cil to extend the benefits of that program. After this established
success and with an understanding of the risks of opioid overdose on too
many New Yorkers, this bill aims to offer a similar program to estab-
lishments beyond the City of New York.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This bill shall take effect on the one hundred twentieth day after it
becomes law.

approvalMessage.text:
APPROVAL MEMORANDUM - No. 72 Chapter 778
 
       MEMORANDUM filed with Senate Bill Number 8633-A, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT to amend the public health law, in relation to establishing
        the nightlife opioid antagonist program"
 
    APPROVED
 
  This bill would establish the voluntary  nightlife  opioid  antagonist
program,  including  access  to opioid antagonists and public reporting.
The State has a robust opioid  antagonist  program  including  both  the
Statewide  Standing Order for pharmacies to carry stocks of Naloxone and
trainings and education by the Department of Health and  the  Office  of
Addiction  Services and Supports. This legislation is a worthy effort to
expand access to these life-saving medications.

  As one of the millions of Americans who has lost a loved  one  to  the
opioid  crisis,  I fully support the goals of this legislation. However,
it would be duplicative and confusing to establish a new program for one
specific industry when State agencies have existing, robust  initiatives
to achieve this worthy goal. I have reached an agreement with the Legis-
lature  to amend this legislation to include nightlife establishments in
our existing opioid antagonist  programs.  This  will  provide  specific
guidelines  to  nightlife  establishments  to  ensure  these places have
access to the opioid antagonists that  they  need  in  life  threatening
situations.
 
  Based on this agreement, I am pleased to sign this bill into law.
 
  This bill is approved.                         (signed) KATHY HOCHUL
 
                                ______

summary: Establishes the nightlife opioid antagonist program to allow certain establishments to apply and receive an opioid antagonist, free of charge, to be administered to patrons, staff or individuals on premises of such establishment in the case of an emergency.
